glossary.definition: A licensed professional who represents the policyholder — not the insurer — in preparing and negotiating a property insurance claim, typically paid a contingency of 10 to 20 percent of the settlement.
A sworn statement of the amount and cause of a loss, which most property policies require the policyholder to submit within a set window. Missing the window can forfeit an otherwise valid claim.
Language inside a policy exclusion that restores coverage in defined circumstances. A denial letter that quotes an exclusion but stops before its carve-back is quoting selectively.
The situation where a loss has more than one cause, at least one covered and one excluded. How a state resolves concurrent causation frequently decides whether the claim is paid.
A policy provision allowing a dispute about the amount of loss — not about coverage — to be resolved by appraisers rather than litigation. It is usually subject to its own demand deadline.
Individualized Education Program. The legally binding document under IDEA setting out a student's special education goals, services and accommodations.

The section of an IEP describing the student's current performance. It frequently names a need that the goals and services then fail to address, which is the most common basis for a successful challenge.
The quantity of special education or related service an IEP commits to, usually stated in a grid. The grid total and the narrative promise disagree more often than expected.
Billing separately for procedures that payer rules require to be billed together as one code, generally producing a higher total than the bundled rate.

The statement a health plan sends showing what was billed, what the plan allowed, what it paid and what the patient owes. It is not a bill, and reconciling it against the provider's bill is where errors surface.
An amendment attached to a policy that modifies the base form. Endorsements frequently contain the provision that decides a claim, and are the most commonly overlooked part of a policy.
A cap inside a policy that applies to a specific category of loss and is lower than the overall policy limit. Mould, water backup and ordinance-or-law coverage are common examples.
A state law setting deadlines by which an insurer must acknowledge, investigate and pay or deny a claim, often with interest or penalties for breach.
Replacement cost less depreciation. Whether a policy pays actual cash value or replacement cost is frequently the largest single dollar difference in a property claim.
The amount withheld from an initial claim payment that becomes payable once repairs are completed and documented. It is often never claimed because nobody tells the policyholder it exists.
The estimating software used across most of the property claims industry. Line-item disagreements between an adjuster's estimate and a contractor's are usually expressed in its terms.
Free Appropriate Public Education. The standard a school district must meet under IDEA, and the legal question underlying most special education disputes.
Least Restrictive Environment. The IDEA requirement that a student be educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate.
The formal notice a district must give when it proposes or refuses to change a student's identification, evaluation or placement. A refusal delivered verbally instead is itself a procedural issue.
An evaluation by a qualified examiner not employed by the district, which a parent may request at public expense when they disagree with the district's evaluation.
The formal dispute mechanism under IDEA, triggering a hearing before an impartial officer. Strict filing deadlines apply and vary by state.
When a provider bills a patient for the difference between their charge and what the plan paid. It is restricted in many situations by federal and state law.
Billing a higher-intensity service code than the care actually delivered supports, producing a larger payment than the encounter warrants.
A payer requirement that a service be approved before it is delivered. A denial for missing prior authorisation is frequently reversible where the requirement was not communicated.

It will not represent anyone. It will not negotiate a claim, attend a meeting, sign a filing or give advice. Where your state requires a licence to act for a policyholder or a family, that licence is yours and the responsibility stays with you.

Every one of these professions is paid on outcome or by the hour, is capacity-limited by one person's reading speed, and turns away work it would like to take. None of them has a demand problem.

They also share a failure mode: the winning argument is usually a contradiction between two documents that nobody had time to read side by side. That is a machine problem wearing a professional's clothes.

blocks.h2: A note on "closed with no payment"
blocks.body:
That statistic is widely quoted and it is worth being precise about, because your clients will quote it back to you. "Closed with no payment" also counts claims that fell below the deductible and claims the policyholder withdrew. Not every one is a wrongful denial.

What the number does show is a trend — 36% to 44% over a decade — that deductibles alone do not explain, and a large population of withdrawn claims, which is often just a homeowner who gave up. Both are your market.

pages.title: How to read an insurance denial letter
pages.h1: How to read an insurance denial letter
pages.description: A denial letter has to do four things. Most do two well and two badly, and the gap between what it cites and what the policy says is where the claim is won. A working method for reading one.
pages.lede: A denial letter is a legal document written by someone who does this all day, addressed to someone doing it for the first time. That asymmetry is the point of it. Here is how to take it apart.

sections.h2: What a denial letter must contain
sections.body:
Requirements vary by state, but a denial letter that is doing its job will tell you four things: what was claimed, what was decided, the specific policy provision relied on, and what the policyholder can do next.

The third is the one that matters and the one most often thin. A letter that says the loss is "not covered under the terms and conditions of your policy" has not cited anything. A letter that says the loss falls under a named exclusion has made a claim you can test against the policy itself.

When the provision is missing or vague, that absence is itself the first thing to write about, because in many states the carrier is required to be specific.

sections.h2: Read the policy in the right order
sections.body:
Policies are not written to be read front to back, and reading them that way is how experienced people still miss things. The order that works:

  1. The declarations page. What is actually covered, the limits, the deductibles, the endorsements attached. Endorsements modify the base form and are frequently where the answer sits.
  2. The insuring agreement. The broad grant of coverage, before anything takes coverage away.
  3. The exclusion the letter cited — and only then. Read it word by word, including its exceptions. Exclusions routinely contain carve-backs that restore coverage, and a carve-back is the single most productive thing to look for.
  4. Definitions. A policy defines its own terms and those definitions override ordinary meaning. Words like "sudden", "accidental", "collapse" and "water damage" are almost always defined and rarely mean what a homeowner assumes.

sections.h2: The four gaps that appear most often
sections.body:
The cited provision does not say what the letter says it says. Read it directly rather than through the letter's paraphrase. This is common enough that it should be the first thing checked, not the last.

An exception inside the exclusion was ignored. Exclusions frequently end with language restoring coverage in defined circumstances. A letter that quotes the exclusion and stops before the carve-back is quoting selectively.

The wrong cause of loss was assigned. Damage often has a sequence — a covered event causes an excluded one, or the reverse. Which one is treated as the cause frequently decides the claim, and how that is resolved depends on your state's approach to concurrent causation.

The investigation did not support the conclusion. If the file shows no inspection, no engineer, or a report that says something different from the letter, the denial rests on nothing.

sections.h2: Build the response around the document, not the grievance
sections.body:
The letter that works is boring. It states the provision, quotes the policy language in full, states the fact, and shows the contradiction. It does not argue about fairness and it does not editorialise.

Structure that survives escalation:

  • The claim, the date, the number.
  • What the denial said, quoted exactly.
  • What the policy says, quoted exactly, in full.
  • The facts, each one attached to the document that evidences it.
  • What you are asking for, specifically.
  • The deadline you are working to, and the statute or provision it comes from.

Everything in that list is a citation. That is not a stylistic preference — a letter where every assertion is traceable is a letter that survives being forwarded to someone senior.

sections.h2: Watch the clock from the first day
sections.body:
Proof-of-loss windows, appraisal demand periods and prompt-payment statutes all run on their own timetables and they vary by state. They are also the most common way a winnable claim is lost, because the deadline passes while the file is being assembled.

Diary every date the day the file opens rather than the day you start working it.

faqs.q: Can a denial be reversed without a lawyer?
faqs.a: Frequently, yes. Many are resolved by a documented response that shows the cited provision does not support the decision. Whether your situation needs a licensed public adjuster or a lawyer depends on your state and the amount at stake.

faqs.q: What if the letter cites no provision at all?
faqs.a: Ask for it in writing, and note the date you asked. In many states a specific reason is required, and a refusal to give one is itself worth documenting.

faqs.q: Does asking for the claim file help?
faqs.a: Often substantially. Inspection notes, photographs and engineer reports frequently do not match the conclusion in the letter. What you can obtain and when depends on your state.

pages.closing: This guide describes how to read documents. It is not legal advice, not insurance advice, and no substitute for a licensed public adjuster or an attorney in your state. Requirements and deadlines vary substantially by jurisdiction.

pages.title: When the IEP does not match the evaluation
pages.h1: When the IEP does not match the evaluation
pages.description: The strongest argument in special education advocacy is usually built from the district's own evaluation: it identified a need that the IEP does not address. How to find that gap and document it.
pages.lede: You rarely need an outside expert to make the argument. The district already wrote the evidence down in its own evaluation — the question is whether the IEP responded to it.

sections.h2: Why the district's own evaluation is the strongest document you have
sections.body:
An outside expert can be argued with. The district's own evaluation cannot be argued with by the district, because they wrote it, they stand behind it, and it was produced by their own staff.

So the comparison that matters is narrow and mechanical: every need, finding and recommendation in the evaluation, against every goal, service and accommodation in the IEP. Anything on the left with nothing on the right is the argument.

Make a two-column table. On the left, every statement in the evaluation that identifies a need — including ones buried in narrative paragraphs rather than in the summary, which is where they hide. On the right, the specific goal, service, accommodation or minute allocation that addresses it.

Three categories come out of this:

  • Addressed. A need with a matching, measurable goal or service. Fine, move on.
  • Named but unaddressed. The evaluation identified it; the IEP mentions it in the present levels and then does nothing about it. This is the most common finding and the most useful.
  • Addressed too thinly. A significant need answered with a token accommodation or a handful of minutes. Harder to argue but often the more consequential problem.

A goal that cannot be measured cannot be enforced later, which means it will not be. Every goal should have four parts: a baseline saying where the student is now, a target, a criterion for success, and a stated method of measurement.

Goals missing the baseline are extremely common and are worth flagging every time. Without a starting point there is no way to demonstrate a year from now that progress did or did not happen — which quietly removes the only mechanism the parent has.

Read what the IEP narrative promises, then add up what the service grid actually allocates. These disagree more often than anyone expects, and the grid is what the school actually delivers.

Check also whether the setting matches the service, and whether the minutes are per week, per month or per cycle — a change of unit is an easy way for a service to shrink without anyone appearing to decide anything.

sections.h2: Write it as a request, not a complaint
sections.body:
The letter that works quotes the evaluation, quotes the IEP, and asks a question that is difficult to answer badly: the evaluation identified X on page 12; I do not see a goal or service addressing X; can you point me to it or add one?

That framing is effective because it is genuinely open. Sometimes the answer is that it is addressed somewhere you did not look, and finding that out costs nothing. When there is no answer, the absence is now documented in writing, which is what matters if the case escalates.

faqs.q: What if the district refuses to reconvene?
faqs.a: Put the request in writing, keep the date, and check your state's required response timeline. A refusal in writing is more useful to you than a verbal agreement.

faqs.q: Do I need an independent evaluation?
faqs.a: Often not, if the district's own evaluation already identifies the need. An independent evaluation matters most when you are disputing the findings themselves rather than the response to them.

faqs.q: How long should the crosswalk take?
faqs.a: By hand, several hours for a substantial evaluation and IEP. It is exactly the kind of exhaustive cross-referencing that is easy to do badly when tired.

pages.closing: This guide describes a document review method. It is not legal advice. Special education law is federal but its procedures vary by state, and a family facing a due process matter should speak to an attorney licensed in their state.

pages.title: How advocates charge, and what it means for capacity
pages.h1: How advocates charge, and what it means for capacity
pages.description: Hourly, contingency and flat fee across public adjusting, special education advocacy and patient advocacy — the published rates, and why every pricing model eventually hits the same capacity ceiling.
pages.lede: Three professions, three pricing models, one ceiling. Everyone in this work eventually runs out of the same thing, and it is not demand.

sections.body:
Published and widely reported rates as of 2026:

  • Public adjusters: 10–20% of the settlement, typically 10–15% on residential property. Florida caps this by statute at 10% in the year following a declared emergency and 20% otherwise.
  • Medical bill negotiators: 10–35% of savings.
  • Property tax appeal firms: 25–50% of first-year savings.
  • Special education advocates: $75–300 per hour; roughly 10–15 hours for a typical case.

Treat these as a guide rather than gospel — a large share of published rate information comes from firms selling the service.

Contingency aligns you with the client and removes the affordability objection entirely, which is why it dominates in claims work. It has one structural weakness: it makes small cases irrational to take.

At 15% of settlement, a $6,000 claim pays $900. If reading the policy and assembling the file takes eight hours, that is $112 an hour before overhead — and the small claim takes nearly as long to read as the large one, because the policy is the same length either way.

So the bottom of the market goes unserved, not because those people do not need help but because the reading time does not scale down with the claim. That is a capacity problem disguised as a pricing problem.

Hourly billing is honest and it caps your income at your available hours. At $150 an hour and 20 billable hours a week, the ceiling is roughly $150,000 a year before overhead, and every hour of reading is an hour not spent in a meeting or on a call.

It also prices out exactly the families most likely to need help — the special education research says this directly, describing cost as a substantial barrier and the system as stacked against low and middle-income families.

Whatever the model, the constraint is the same: one person can only read so much. Not client acquisition, not competition, not pricing. Reading.

Which means the only real ways to grow are to raise rates until demand falls away, hire and supervise other people, or reduce the reading time per case. The third is the only one that also lets you serve people who cannot pay full freight.

sections.h2: Working the arithmetic on any tool
sections.body:
The calculation is short. Multiply your hourly rate by the hours a tool saves per month and compare it to the price. At $150 an hour, a $299 tool needs to save two hours a month to break even; at $250 an hour it needs to save 72 minutes.

The more useful question is the second one: what would you do with the freed hours? More full-fee cases raises income. Sliding-scale cases raises reach. Both are better answers than working fewer hours, though that is a legitimate answer too.

faqs.q: Is contingency allowed in every state?
faqs.a: For public adjusting, it is standard but regulated, and several states cap the percentage — Florida's caps are the best-known. Rules differ by profession and state; check yours.

faqs.q: Should I switch from hourly to contingency?
faqs.a: It depends on your case mix and your cash position. Contingency means carrying costs until settlement, which is a real constraint for a solo practice.

faqs.q: How do sliding-scale practices survive?
faqs.a: Usually by cross-subsidising from full-fee cases, which only works if the full-fee cases are efficient enough to leave room.

pages.closing: Rates cited are drawn from published industry and practitioner sources in 2026, several of which are published by firms that sell these services. They are indicative of the market rather than authoritative, and none was independently verified.

pages.title: About Countercite
pages.description: Countercite exists because institutions automated their side of every dispute and the people representing individuals did not. Built for the advocates already doing that work.

blocks.lede: Both sides of a dispute were supposed to get better software. Only one side did.

blocks.h2: The asymmetry
blocks.body:
In the first quarter of 2026, 95.2% of insurtech funding went to AI companies — and industry reporting described that wave as aimed at infrastructure providers rather than at anything consumer-facing. Sixty-five percent of insurers planned scaled AI claims agents for the year. Over the same decade in which that capability was built, the share of claims closed with no payment at the five largest home insurers went from 36% to 44%.

The same shape holds elsewhere. School districts have compliance software. Hospitals have revenue-cycle systems. On the other side stands one person, doing this once, usually during the worst month of their life — or the advocate they hired, working from a highlighter and a Saturday.

Countercite is built for that advocate. Not to replace them, which is neither possible nor legal in most of this work, but to make the reading fast enough that they can take the cases they currently turn away.

blocks.h2: What we learned from the last company that tried this
blocks.body:
In February 2025 the Federal Trade Commission finalised an order requiring DoNotPay to pay $193,000 and to stop advertising that its service performed like a real lawyer. A parallel class action settled for the same amount. The finding was specific: the company never tested whether its system worked at the level it claimed, and never retained attorneys to check.

It had users. It had press. It had revenue. What it did not have was evidence.

So we do three things because of that order. We measure outcomes from the first customer. We keep the licensed professional in the loop wherever the law requires one. And we never claim to be the professional — Countercite is a tool in your practice, and the name on the work is yours.

The documents you upload. Insurance policies, denial letters, endorsements, correspondence, and anything else you choose to add to a case.

These documents commonly contain your name, your address, the address of the insured property, your policy number, your claim number, dates and details of a loss, and sometimes financial or medical information you did not necessarily think about when you uploaded them. We treat everything in an uploaded document as sensitive, because we cannot know in advance which parts are.

Your account information. Your name, email address, the password hash, your plan, and if you are a licensed professional, the licence number and state you choose to give us.

Payment information. Handled entirely by our payment processor. We never see or store your card number. We see the last four digits, the card brand, and whether a payment succeeded.

A clear refund promise you keep is worth more than a paragraph of conditions, and it is one of the cheapest ways to stay clear of a consumer-protection complaint.

Price changes. If we change the price of your plan we will tell you at least to be completed: 30 days before it applies to you, by email. If you do not want the new price, cancel before it takes effect and you will not be charged it.

Fair use. Our plans are flat and unmetered on purpose, because a tool people ration is a tool people stop using. That only works if nobody uses it at a scale nobody anticipated. If your usage goes past to be completed: state the actual ceiling, e.g. 500 documents or 25,000 pages in a month, we will contact you and work out a fair arrangement. We will not cut you off without talking to you first.

Taxes are yours, where any apply.

6. Your documents belong to you

You keep every right you have in the documents you upload and in the letters Countercite drafts for you. Uploading something does not give us ownership of it.

You give us permission to store and process your documents for one purpose only: running the analysis you asked for and producing the output you asked for. That permission ends when you delete the document or close your account.

We do not use your documents to train any model, ours or anyone else's. We do not sell your documents or your data. We do not share them for advertising. The PRIVACY-POLICY.md document sets out exactly who touches a document, for how long, and what happens to it afterwards.

7. Confidentiality

We treat everything you upload as confidential. We only disclose it if you tell us to, or if we are legally required to, and if we are legally required to we will tell you unless the law forbids it.

The privacy policy is the detailed version of this section, including the list of the outside services that process your documents.

8. What we do not promise

Countercite is careful software and it is still software. It will sometimes miss a contradiction that a person would find, and it will sometimes raise something that turns out not to matter.

We measure this rather than assert it. Our accuracy figures, how they are produced and what they cover are published at to be completed: URL of the accuracy or measurement page. When we publish a number, we publish what it was measured on and when. If we cannot show you the measurement, we do not make the claim.

We do not promise that Countercite will find every discrepancy in your documents, that your appeal will succeed, that your insurer will change its decision, or that you will be paid anything. Nobody can promise that, and anyone who does is telling you something they cannot support.

Beyond what is written in these terms, Countercite is provided as it is. To the extent the law allows, we do not make other warranties, including implied ones about merchantability or fitness for a particular purpose. Some of those protections cannot be waived where you live, and where that is true, this paragraph does not take them away from you.

9. Limits on what we owe you

This section is written in two parts, because our customers are two different kinds of people and the law treats them differently.

If you are an individual using Countercite for your own insurance claim:

If we are responsible for a loss you suffer, what we owe you is capped at the greater of the total amount you paid us in the twelve months before the problem, or to be completed: a floor figure, e.g. $500. A cap of zero, or a cap of one month's fee, is the kind of clause a court is most likely to strike out.

We are not responsible for lost profits, lost claim proceeds, or other indirect losses.

This cap does not apply, and we do not try to limit our responsibility, for: fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence, personal injury, or anything else that the law of your state does not permit us to limit. If a court decides any part of this section goes further than the law allows, that part is reduced to what the law allows and the rest still stands.

If you are a business or a licensed professional using Countercite in your practice:

The same cap applies, with the same carve-outs. In addition, you accept that you review and adopt Countercite's output as your own work before you use it with a client, and that your professional responsibility for that work stays with you, where it already sat before you started using us.

10. If something goes wrong between us

Talk to us first. Email support@countercite.app with what happened. Most things get sorted out here, and we would rather fix a problem than argue about one. We will respond within to be completed: 10 business days.

Where disputes get resolved. These terms are governed by the law of to be completed: your state, likely Texas, and disputes go to the state or federal courts of to be completed: your county and state.

But if you are an individual consumer, you are not required to travel. You may bring a claim in the courts where you live, and we will not object on the ground that it is the wrong place. You may also use small claims court in your own area for anything within its limits, and we will not try to move it.

to be completed: Decide whether you want an arbitration clause here. The honest position: consumer arbitration clauses are widely used and widely enforced, and they are also one of the things a regulator points at when it decides a business is avoiding accountability. In the North Carolina LegalZoom settlement the bar required local venue for consumers. A solo operator with few customers gets less from an arbitration clause than a large company does, and gives up more goodwill. Consider leaving it out.

11. Ending the agreement

Where we reasonably can, we will tell you first and give you a chance to fix it. If we close your account for a reason that is not your fault, we refund the unused part of what you paid.

When your account closes, you can export your documents and findings for to be completed: 30 days. After that we delete them, on the schedule in the privacy policy.

13. The rest of it

agreement** between us about Countercite, and they replace anything said earlier.

pages.title: Glossary of advocacy, claims and IEP terms
pages.description: Plain definitions of the terms that decide cases: carve-backs, concurrent causation, proof of loss, present levels, service minutes, unbundling, prior authorisation and more.

blocks.lede: The vocabulary that decides cases, defined plainly. Most of these are terms an institution uses correctly and assumes the other side does not understand.

blocks.h2: Terms
blocks.body:
Actual cash value

Replacement cost less depreciation. Whether a policy pays actual cash value or replacement cost is frequently the largest single dollar difference in a property claim.

Appraisal

A policy provision allowing a dispute about the amount of loss — not about coverage — to be resolved by appraisers rather than litigation. It is usually subject to its own demand deadline.

Balance billing

When a provider bills a patient for the difference between their charge and what the plan paid. It is restricted in many situations by federal and state law.

Carve-back

Language inside a policy exclusion that restores coverage in defined circumstances. A denial letter that quotes an exclusion but stops before its carve-back is quoting selectively.

Concurrent causation

The situation where a loss has more than one cause, at least one covered and one excluded. How a state resolves concurrent causation frequently decides whether the claim is paid.

Due process complaint

The formal dispute mechanism under IDEA, triggering a hearing before an impartial officer. Strict filing deadlines apply and vary by state.

Endorsement

An amendment attached to a policy that modifies the base form. Endorsements frequently contain the provision that decides a claim, and are the most commonly overlooked part of a policy.

Explanation of benefits

The statement a health plan sends showing what was billed, what the plan allowed, what it paid and what the patient owes. It is not a bill, and reconciling it against the provider's bill is where errors surface.

FAPE

Free Appropriate Public Education. The standard a school district must meet under IDEA, and the legal question underlying most special education disputes.

IEP

Individualized Education Program. The legally binding document under IDEA setting out a student's special education goals, services and accommodations.

Independent educational evaluation

An evaluation by a qualified examiner not employed by the district, which a parent may request at public expense when they disagree with the district's evaluation.

LRE

Least Restrictive Environment. The IDEA requirement that a student be educated with non-disabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate.

Present levels

The section of an IEP describing the student's current performance. It frequently names a need that the goals and services then fail to address, which is the most common basis for a successful challenge.

Prior authorisation

A payer requirement that a service be approved before it is delivered. A denial for missing prior authorisation is frequently reversible where the requirement was not communicated.

Prior written notice

The formal notice a district must give when it proposes or refuses to change a student's identification, evaluation or placement. A refusal delivered verbally instead is itself a procedural issue.

Prompt payment statute

A state law setting deadlines by which an insurer must acknowledge, investigate and pay or deny a claim, often with interest or penalties for breach.

Proof of loss

A sworn statement of the amount and cause of a loss, which most property policies require the policyholder to submit within a set window. Missing the window can forfeit an otherwise valid claim.

Public adjuster

A licensed professional who represents the policyholder — not the insurer — in preparing and negotiating a property insurance claim, typically paid a contingency of 10 to 20 percent of the settlement.

Recoverable depreciation

The amount withheld from an initial claim payment that becomes payable once repairs are completed and documented. It is often never claimed because nobody tells the policyholder it exists.

Service minutes

The quantity of special education or related service an IEP commits to, usually stated in a grid. The grid total and the narrative promise disagree more often than expected.

Sub-limit

A cap inside a policy that applies to a specific category of loss and is lower than the overall policy limit. Mould, water backup and ordinance-or-law coverage are common examples.

Unbundling

Billing separately for procedures that payer rules require to be billed together as one code, generally producing a higher total than the bundled rate.

Upcoding

Billing a higher-intensity service code than the care actually delivered supports, producing a larger payment than the encounter warrants.

Xactimate

The estimating software used across most of the property claims industry. Line-item disagreements between an adjuster's estimate and a contractor's are usually expressed in its terms.

pages.title: What Countercite is not | Countercite
pages.description: Countercite is not a law firm, not a licensed adjuster and not a medical provider. The exact limits of what it does, stated once, in full.

blocks.lede: Countercite is not a law firm, not a licensed adjuster and not a medical provider. The exact limits of what it does, stated once, in full.

blocks.body:
A note before you read this.

This is a starting draft, written without a lawyer. The wording below is deliberately borrowed rather than invented: some of it tracks the words of a Texas statute, some of it tracks a California statute as restated by the online legal forms industry, and some of it tracks conditions a state bar imposed on a much larger company. Borrowed language is safer than clever language, because somebody has already argued about it.

The reasoning behind each choice is in 00-LEGAL-POSTURE.md §1.2 and §1.5. Every to be completed: ... marker is something the owner still has to complete.

Why placement is half the job

In Unauthorized Practice of Law Committee v. Parsons Technology the software's disclaimer appeared only on first start-up. It was not on the packaging and it did not reappear on later uses. The district court enjoined the product anyway. Texas then passed the safe harbour now at Tex. Gov't Code § 81.101(c), which protects software only where the product "clearly and conspicuously" states it is not a substitute for the advice of an attorney.

So the statute's price is conspicuousness, and the case that produced the statute is a case about a disclaimer that was easy to miss. A disclaimer sitting in a footer link is not conspicuous. The placements below are more aggressive than a designer will want them to be. That is the point.

Formatting rules that apply to every disclaimer here

  1. Same size as surrounding body text or larger. Never smaller. Never grey

on grey.

  1. Never collapsed behind a link, an accordion, a tooltip, or a "learn more".

The words must be on the page.

  1. Never inside a scrolling box the customer can skip past.
  2. Never removed for returning users. D1 and D3 appear every time, not once.
  3. Present in the exported file itself, not only on the screen that made it.

A PDF gets forwarded; the screen does not travel with it.

  1. Identical wording everywhere. Do not paraphrase per page. Copy these

strings. A variant is a variant somebody has to defend.

The disclaimers

D1. The master disclaimer

Exact text:

Countercite is not a law firm and is not a licensed public insurance adjuster. Countercite is not a substitute for the advice of an attorney. We cannot give you any kind of advice, explanation, opinion or recommendation about your legal rights, remedies, defences, options, choice of forms or strategy. Countercite reports what your own documents say and shows you the page. What that means for your claim is your decision, or your professional's.

Where it must appear:

LocationForm
Every page of the websiteFooter, full text, not a link
The pricing page, above the plansFull text, in the body of the page, not the footer
The signup and checkout screens, above the payment buttonFull text
Inside the application, footer of every screenFull text
Every exported document, first pageFull text

Why this wording. The middle sentence tracks Tex. Gov't Code § 81.101(c) almost verbatim, which is what the safe harbour asks for. The list that follows ("advice, explanation, opinion or recommendation about legal rights, remedies, defences, options, choice of forms or strategy") tracks the prohibited-acts list at Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 6411, which is the language the online legal forms industry adopted for exactly this reason. Both citations are and neither statute was read in the original.

The checkout placement is not optional. Parsons' disclaimer failed partly because it was not on the packaging. Checkout is this product's packaging.

D2. First-run acknowledgement

Exact text:

Before you start, three things.

1. Countercite is not a lawyer and not an adjuster. It cannot tell you whether your claim is valid, whether your denial was correct, or whether an appeal will succeed. It is not a substitute for the advice of an attorney.

2. Every finding points at a page in your own documents. Open the page. Countercite will sometimes miss something a person would catch, and will sometimes raise something that turns out not to matter. Check the work before you rely on it.

3. You send it, not us. Countercite never contacts your insurance company. It produces a draft. You edit it, you approve it, and it goes out under your name.

What you upload here is not protected by attorney-client privilege, because we are not attorneys. How we handle your documents is in the privacy policy.

[ ] I have read this [ Continue ]

Where it must appear: a modal on first login, before the first upload. The checkbox must be unticked by default and the Continue button disabled until it is ticked. Record the timestamp and the account against the acknowledgement, and keep that record. Show it again after any material change to this wording.

Why. This is the point where the customer forms their expectation of what they bought. It is also the record that proves what they were told, which is worth more than the modal itself.

D3. On the findings screen

Exact text, immediately above the list of findings:

These are observations about your documents, not conclusions about your claim. Each one shows you a page and a passage so you can check it. None of them means your denial was wrong, or that you are owed anything. Countercite cannot tell you that.

Where: above the findings list, every time, on every case. Not dismissible.

Why. This is the screen where a customer is most likely to read a finding as a verdict, because it looks like one. 00-LEGAL-POSTURE.md §1.3 walks through the six-sentence ladder from safe description to prohibited advice. This banner sits on top of the ladder.

D4. On the appeal letter builder

Exact text, above the draft:

This is a draft for you to edit, not a finished letter. It quotes your denial letter and your policy and asks your insurer to explain or reconsider. It does not argue that your denial was wrong, because Countercite is not in a position to say that. Read every paragraph. Change anything you want. Delete anything you are not comfortable putting your name to.

Countercite does not send this. When you are finished, download it and send it yourself.

Where: at the top of the letter builder, and above the export button.

Additional interface requirements, which matter more than the words:

  • Every paragraph is individually editable in a real text field.
  • Every paragraph must be individually approved before export, in the same

way canExport() in the engine already requires every finding to be reviewed.

  • **There is no send button, no email integration, no fax integration, and no

"we'll mail it for you" option.** Not now, not later. Adding one changes what this product legally is. See 00-LEGAL-POSTURE.md §1.2 on TIKD.

D5. On every exported document

Exact text, in a bordered box at the top of page one, and repeated as a footer on every page:

Top of page one:

Prepared using Countercite, to be completed: legal entity name, to be completed: city, state, countercite.app.

Countercite is not a law firm, is not a licensed public insurance adjuster, and is not a substitute for the advice of an attorney. This document was generated from documents supplied by the sender and was reviewed and approved by the sender before it was sent. Countercite did not send it, did not contact any insurer, and offers no opinion on whether any claim is payable.

Footer on every page:

Prepared using Countercite. Not legal advice. Not a substitute for the advice of an attorney. countercite.app

Why. The exported file is the only part of this product that reaches a third party, which means it is the only part a regulator or an insurer's counsel is likely to see first. It has to identify itself, name the company and the address, and say what it is not, without the surrounding website. The name-and-address requirement mirrors condition 4 of the North Carolina consent judgment .

D6. Wherever an accuracy figure appears

Exact text, immediately adjacent to the number, not in a footnote:

This figure comes from to be completed: describe the dataset in one line, e.g. "138 findings across 20 real denial letters, graded by a licensed Texas public adjuster in [[FILL: month, year"]]. It describes how Countercite performed on those documents. It does not predict how it will perform on yours, and it says nothing about whether any appeal succeeded.

Where: next to every accuracy, hours-saved or confirmation-rate number, on the site, in a deck, in an email, in a social post, anywhere.

The rule behind the rule: if the dataset sentence cannot be written, the number cannot be published. See NO-GUARANTEE-AND-TESTING-POLICY.md.

D7. On the public adjuster pages

Exact text:

Countercite is software licensed to you for use in your own practice. It is not a licensed public insurance adjuster, does not adjust claims, does not negotiate with carriers, and never contacts an insurer. It does not act on behalf of any insured. Your work product, and your professional responsibility for it, remain yours.

Where: on /for/public-adjusters, and on any page, email or deck aimed at licensed professionals.

Why. Every state's public adjuster statute catches a person who holds themselves out as an adjuster, not only one who acts as one. Texas § 4102.001, Florida § 626.854, California art. 3 and 215 ILCS 5/1515 all include a holding-out prong . Marketing copy is where a holding-out problem would be created, not code.

D8. Wherever a customer's testimonial or story appears

Exact text, adjacent to the quote:

One customer's experience. Results depend on the documents, the policy and the insurer, and are not typical of anything. Countercite does not promise an outcome.

Where: next to every testimonial, case study, screenshot of a result, and before-and-after.

The placement map

One row per surface. Use this as the QA checklist before launch and before any redesign.

SurfaceD1D2D3D4D5D6D7D8
Home pageFooterIf a number appearsIf a quote appears
Pricing pageIn body, above plansIf a number appears
/for/public-adjustersFooterYesIf a quote appears
Guides and glossaryFooter
Signup / checkoutAbove the pay button
First loginModal, must acknowledge
Upload screenFooter
Findings screenFooterAbove the list
Letter builderFooterAbove the draft
Exported PDF or DOCXPage 1 box + every page footer
Marketing emailSignature blockIf a number appearsIf sent to adjustersIf a quote appears
Deck or PDF sent to a prospectSlide 1 or page 1If a number appearsIf a quote appears

What marketing may never say

These are not style preferences. Each maps to a rule in 00-LEGAL-POSTURE.md §1.4.2 and to a pattern in the blocked-phrase fixture.

Never, in any copy, anywhere:

  • "AI lawyer", "robot lawyer", "your AI attorney", "AI adjuster", "virtual

adjuster", "digital advocate"

  • "as good as a lawyer", "as good as an adjuster", "replaces your attorney",

"instead of hiring a public adjuster", "you don't need a lawyer"

  • "we'll fight your insurer", "we negotiate for you", "we handle your claim",

"we deal with the carrier"

  • "guaranteed", "we guarantee", "get what you're owed", "recover up to $X",

"win your appeal", any win rate, any success percentage

  • "no win, no fee", any percentage of a settlement, any contingent pricing
  • "legal advice", except inside the fixed sentence "this is not legal advice"

A note on "AI-powered". PLAN.md §4 already says AI is never the headline claim, and the reason is the DoNotPay order. Keep it that way. The headline is the citation to the page, which is a claim about a mechanism and is verifiable. Any capability claim about a model is a claim the FTC expects substantiated by competent and reliable evidence .

Pre-launch check

Someone should be able to run this in an hour.

  1. Load every page in dist/countercite/. Confirm the D1 footer text is

present and identical on each one.

  1. Confirm D1 appears in the body of the pricing page and above the payment

button at checkout, not only in the footer.

  1. Confirm the D2 modal blocks the first upload and records the acknowledgement.
  2. Confirm D3 and D4 are not dismissible and reappear on every case.
  3. Export a document. Confirm D5 is on page one and in the footer of every page.
  4. Search the whole site and every email template for every phrase in the "never

say" list above. Zero hits.

  1. Find every number on the site. Confirm each has its D6 dataset sentence, or

delete the number.

  1. Run the blocked-phrase fixture from 00-LEGAL-POSTURE.md §1.4.3 over every

string in the engine and every page of the site. Zero hits outside the fixed disclaimer strings.

pages.description: What gets measured, on which documents, how the numbers are recorded, and what may be said about them publicly. Written before any number existed.

blocks.lede: What gets measured, on which documents, how the numbers are recorded, and what may be said about them publicly. Written before any number existed.

blocks.body:
How Countercite measures itself, and what it is allowed to say as a result.

A note before you read this.

This is a starting draft, written without a lawyer. Unlike the other documents in this folder, this one is mostly an internal operating rule rather than a customer contract, and it is the one the owner should follow whether or not anyone ever reviews it. Every to be completed: ... marker is something the owner still has to complete.

1. Why this document exists

In February 2025 the FTC finalised an order against DoNotPay. The company paid $193,000, had to notify every consumer who subscribed between 2021 and 2023, and accepted a standing prohibition on claiming its service could substitute for a professional without competent and reliable evidence .

The charge was not that the product was bad. The charge was that the company never tested whether it performed at the level of a human lawyer, never retained attorneys to check the accuracy of its law-related features, and advertised anyway .

That is a self-inflicted wound, and it is the cheapest one on the entire risk register to avoid. The FTC has since brought more than a dozen further Section 5 actions under Operation AI Comply, on the same theory: a claim about what AI can do must be substantiated by competent and reliable evidence, and that enforcement has continued through 2025 and into 2026 .

The rule this whole document reduces to: no claim without a record.

PLAN.md §8 already says the first two accuracy metrics are tracked from customer one and published, and that this is the direct lesson of the DoNotPay order. This document is the machinery for doing it.

2. The gate before any selling

No paying customer before the corpus is graded. This is already PLAN.md §7 days 1 to 30, and it is repeated here because it is the load-bearing commitment.

Corpus20 real denial letters, each with the policy it refers to
SourcePublic consumer-complaint threads, law firm example pages, and documents contributed with written permission
GraderA licensed public insurance adjuster, named, with a licence number and state. to be completed: name, licence number, state
Paid?to be completed: yes or no, and how much. Record it. A paid grader is fine; an undisclosed relationship is not
MethodThe grader reads each letter and policy independently and lists the discrepancies they find. Countercite's findings are then compared to that list
RecordedPer finding: confirmed, false positive, or missed. Raw records retained per §6

Kill criterion, from PLAN.md §11 and not renegotiable after the fact: if findings confirmed by the professional come in below 70%, do not sell it. Fix the engine or kill the business.

Why an adjuster rather than a lawyer. DoNotPay's specific failure was not retaining attorneys to check law-related features. Countercite's claim is narrower: that its findings are the ones a working professional would make about two documents. A licensed public adjuster is the right grader for that claim, and the claim must be worded to match the grader. See §5.

3. What gets measured

Tied directly to PLAN.md §8. The first three are the ones that appear in public claims. The rest are operating metrics and are not advertised.

MetricTargetDefinition, tightlyPublishable?
Findings confirmed by the professional>85%Of all findings Countercite surfaces on a case, the share the reviewing professional marks confirmed rather than dismissedYes, with dataset
False positives per case<2Findings marked dismissed by the reviewer, divided by casesYes, with dataset
False negatives per case<0.5Discrepancies the grader found that Countercite did not surface, divided by cases. Measured by re-running closed cases where the answer is knownYes, with dataset, and it must be published alongside the other two. Publishing a confirmation rate without a miss rate is the shape of a misleading claim
Hours saved per case>4Self-reported by the customer, in their own wordsOnly as an attributed customer statement, never as a company claim. See §7
Activation: first real case within 7 days>70%Operating metricNo
Monthly churn<4%Operating metricNo
Approach to trial>10%Operating metricNo
Trial to paid>30%Operating metricNo

On the false negative. PLAN.md §8 contains a correction the owner made against himself: a false positive is visible and annoying, while a missed contradiction is invisible until the claim settles low with the professional's name on it. That correction is also why the miss rate has to be published rather than held back. A number that only flatters is a number a regulator reads as a selection.

What is never measured and never claimed: whether appeals succeed, how much anyone recovered, or how Countercite compares to a lawyer or an adjuster. We do not have that data, we cannot get it reliably, and claiming it is the DoNotPay fact pattern exactly.

4. Whose documents the measurements come from

Three sources, and the rules differ for each.

4.1 The graded corpus (pre-launch)

Public documents and documents contributed with written permission. Every contributed document needs a record of who gave it, when, and on what terms. to be completed: keep this as a simple list. Name, date, what was contributed, and the words they agreed to.

4.2 The founding cohort (first 20 customers)

PLAN.md §5 prices the founding cohort at $199/month locked for life in exchange for a testimonial after 60 days and the right to quote their numbers. That exchange has to be written down, because an undisclosed price concession in return for a testimonial is a disclosure problem under the FTC's endorsement rules.

Requirements:

  • Written consent, obtained separately from the terms of service, saying

what may be quoted and how they may be identified.

  • The consideration disclosed wherever the testimonial appears. The plain

version: "[Name] receives a reduced founding-customer rate. They were not paid for this statement." Adjust to whatever is actually true.

  • The customer may withdraw consent at any time, and the quote comes down.
  • No editing that changes meaning. Trimming for length is fine. Trimming a

qualifier is not.

4.3 Ongoing production measurement (every customer)

Every finding a customer marks confirmed or dismissed through the existing review gate is a data point. This is a by-product of a feature that already exists in the engine, which is why the measurement costs nothing to run.

  • Aggregate only. Published production numbers are counts and rates across

customers. No customer's documents, cases or identity appear in any published figure.

  • Opt-out available. A customer who does not want their review outcomes in

the aggregate can say so. to be completed: build the toggle, or state plainly in the privacy policy that aggregate counts are used and cannot be separated.

  • False negatives cannot be measured in production, because nobody knows

what was missed. They are measured only on the graded corpus and on re-runs of closed cases, and any published miss rate must say which.

5. How results are recorded: the claims register

One row per published claim. No row, no claim. Keep it as a file in the repository so it is versioned, dated, and impossible to quietly edit.

Suggested location: innovation/legal/claims-register.md, created when the first measurement exists.

Each entry:

FieldWhat goes in it
Claim IDCW-2026-001 and upward
The exact sentenceWord for word as it will appear in public. Not a summary of it
The numberThe figure, with its denominator
DatasetWhat it was measured on, with n. "138 findings across 20 denial letters and their policies"
PeriodThe dates the data covers
Who graded itName, role, licence number and state where applicable. "The founder" is an acceptable answer for operating metrics and is not acceptable for accuracy claims
Relationship to usPaid, unpaid, customer, founding customer, independent
MethodTwo or three sentences. Enough that someone else could repeat it
Raw data locationPath to the file holding the underlying records
Where publishedEvery page, email, deck and post the sentence appears on
Approved by / dateThe owner, with the date
Review dueThe date this claim must be re-measured or withdrawn. See §8

A worked example, to be replaced with a real one:

6. Keeping the substantiation

  • Raw records are kept for at least to be completed: 3 years after the claim stops

being published. Grader worksheets, per-finding outcomes, the dated export of the production data, and the consent records.

  • Nothing is overwritten. A re-measurement is a new claim ID, and the old one

is marked superseded with its date, not deleted.

  • Customer documents are not part of the substantiation record. Keep the

grades, the counts and the method. Delete the documents on the ordinary retention schedule in the privacy policy. The evidence is the measurement, not the underlying files.

7. What may be advertised

Permitted, with a register entry and the D6 dataset sentence from DISCLAIMERS.md beside it:

  • The confirmation rate, the false-positive rate and the false-negative rate,

published together, with the dataset and the date.

  • A description of what the software does mechanically: that every finding cites

a page and a passage in the customer's own documents; that the engine reports where a denial letter quotes a provision in part; that it refuses to report a finding it cannot locate. These are claims about a mechanism and they are verifiable by using the product. They still need to be true.

  • A customer's own words about their own experience, attributed, with any

consideration disclosed, and with the D8 disclaimer beside it.

  • Prices, plan contents, the fair use ceiling, and anything else factual about

the offering.

Permitted only in this form: hours saved. Never "Countercite saves you six hours a case." Always "[Name], a public adjuster in [city], told us it saved them about six hours on a hail claim in March," with D8 beside it.

8. What may never be advertised

  • Any outcome claim. Win rates, success rates, reversal rates, dollars

recovered, "get what you're owed", "we'll get your claim paid".

  • Any comparison to a professional. Better than, as good as, replaces,

instead of hiring, "you don't need a lawyer". This is the exact claim the DoNotPay order prohibits without competent and reliable evidence, and we will never have that evidence because we will never run that test.

  • Any accuracy number without its dataset sentence and its register entry.
  • A confirmation rate published without the miss rate.
  • Any capability claim about the model as the headline. PLAN.md §4 already

rules out "AI-powered" as the lead, and this is the reason.

  • Any number from a demo, a hand-picked example, or a single impressive case

presented as typical.

  • Any figure carried forward past its review date.

9. Before anything is published

Six checks. They take fifteen minutes and they are the whole policy in practice.

  1. Does every number in this piece have a claims register entry?
  2. Does the D6 dataset sentence sit next to each one, in the body, not a

footnote?

  1. If a confirmation rate appears, does the miss rate appear with it?
  2. Does any sentence compare Countercite to a lawyer or an adjuster? Remove it.
  3. Does any sentence promise, predict or imply an outcome? Remove it.
  4. Run the blocked-phrase fixture from 00-LEGAL-POSTURE.md §1.4.3 over the

copy. Zero hits.

10. When a claim goes stale

Every claim carries a review date, and no review date is more than 12 months out. On that date the claim is either re-measured with fresh data under a new ID, or taken down everywhere it appears.

"Everywhere" includes the site, sales emails, decks, the press page, and social posts. to be completed: keep the list of publication locations current in the register, because a claim you cannot find is a claim you cannot withdraw.

If a re-measurement produces a worse number, publish the worse number or publish nothing. Quietly keeping the old figure while knowing the new one is the behaviour the DoNotPay order exists to punish.
